title: Pontifical dispute: does faith merit justification de congruo?
source_text: XLV. Inter se disputant Theologi Pontificii, An fides, saltem de congruo, non mereatur justificationem. Et quidem eorum nonnulli pretendunt fidem neque de condigno, neque de congruo mereri remissionem peccatorum, & primam quam vocant justificationem, qua homo ex peccatore & non justo fit justus, idque quia Concilium Tridentinum simpliciter excludit a fide meritum justificationis, neque ullam hac in re distinctionem adhibet; qui in sententia est Thomas Stapletonus prolegomenis in librum 5. de Justificatione. Alii vero putant Concilium Tridentinum excludere solum meritum de condigno, non vero negare quin fides de congruo mereri possit justificationem hominis peccatoris per fidem Christum amplectentis, quae est Bellarmini & Vasquezii sententia.
pass_a_gloss: Among themselves the Pontifical theologians dispute whether faith, at least de congruo, does not merit justification. And indeed some of them contend that faith merits neither de condigno nor de congruo the remission of sins and the first justification, as they call it, by which a man from a sinner and unjust becomes just—and that because the Council of Trent simply excludes from faith the merit of justification and applies no distinction in this matter; of which opinion is Thomas Stapleton in the Prolegomena to book 5 On Justification. But others think the Council of Trent excludes only merit de condigno, and does not deny that faith can merit de congruo the justification of a sinful man through faith embracing Christ—which is the opinion of Bellarmine and Vasquez.
pass_b_english: Rome divided: Stapleton—faith merits neither de condigno nor de congruo.
Bellarmine/Vasquez—Trent bars only condign merit; congruous merit of faith allowed.

choices.why: Scholastic merit pair; Trent's scope disputed.
